prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I woke from a bird hitting the window, almost, I thought, hard enough to break it. The sun rose knowingly. I slid the sash up and stuck my head out like someone in an Italian movie. A flicker lay on its back—stunned—but it was blinking steady as a railroad crossing. Was there misery to put out? Would it come to its "senses"? I thought where were you when bark beetles killed half my trees? Then I remembered, sleepily, reading that flickers mostly eat ants. I went back to sleep for half an hour, and dreamed, as I often do, of horses. When next I looked, the bird still lay still, still blinking. Maybe, I thought, it can't roll over. So I went down and rolled it over. Terrified by my touch, it came to life and flop- hopped down the hill into some sagebrush. It didn't fly, but it didn't seem broken, either. I tried to find it later. No luck. Whether it lived and flew off, or died thrust into a bush, was, apparently, none of my business. If it were thrust into a bush, I knew the ants wouldn't wait for the guest of honor to start dinner.

outputs.L2: A bird striking the window jolted me awake—with such force, I imagined, that it might have shattered the glass. Outside, the sun climbed as if it knew something. Raising the window sash, I leaned out the way a character might in an Italian film. Below, a flicker sprawled on its back, apparently dazed, yet its eyes flashed open and shut with the regularity of a railroad signal. Should I end its suffering? Might it recover on its own? I found myself wondering where this creature had been while bark beetles were destroying half the trees on my property. And if it had died there in the bush, I understood full well that the ants wouldn't hold off—they'd begin their feast without waiting for their guest of honor.

# An Encounter with a Flicker

I was awakened by a sharp crack against the window—the unmistakable sound of a bird striking the glass. When I went to investigate, I found a flicker lying on its back on the ground below, stunned but still alive, its eyes blinking slowly against the light.

As I stood watching the bird, my thoughts drifted, unbidden, to the bark beetles that had killed half the trees on my property. I felt the familiar surge of resentment rise in me—these small destroyers that had done such damage. But then I remembered something that softened my mood: flickers, unlike many woodpeckers, feed mostly on ants rather than on the beetles I had been cursing. There was no grudge to hold against this particular creature.

I left the bird to recover and lay down for a nap. I dreamed of horses—vivid, moving things—and when I woke and returned to the window, I saw that the flicker still lay motionless where it had fallen. Concerned, I went down to it, thinking I would gently roll it over onto its feet.

But the moment my hand touched it, the bird startled back to life. It flop-hopped away from me, scrambling into the cover of the sagebrush. It could not manage to fly, yet nothing about it appeared broken or beyond repair. It simply needed distance, and time.

Later, I went looking for the flicker but could not find it anywhere among the brush. In the end, I had to accept that whatever became of the bird—whether it recovered and flew off, or met some quieter end in the sage—was beyond my knowing and beyond my control.
outputs.L4:
# The Flicker

I was woken this morning by a sudden, violent crash against my window—a sound so sharp and unexpected that I bolted upright before I fully understood what had happened. When I went to the glass and looked down, I saw the bird lying on the ground below: a flicker, its speckled breast turned toward the sky, one wing crumpled beneath it. It was stunned, utterly still, and I could not tell from that distance whether it was alive or dead.

For a long while I simply stood and watched it. There is something in such a moment that arrests you, that pulls you out of your ordinary morning thoughts and fixes you on the small drama unfolding below. I found myself contemplating its fate, wondering whether it would rise again or whether I had witnessed the last flicker of its life against the pane. The bird did not move. The minutes stretched on, and still it lay there, immobile, as if suspended between one world and the next.

At last I could bear the not-knowing no longer. I went downstairs and out into the cool air and crossed the ground to where the creature lay. Kneeling, I reached out and, as gently as I could, rolled the immobile bird over to see if any life remained in it.

The instant my fingers touched it, the flicker exploded back into being. Terrified, jolted awake by my touch, it scrambled upright and hopped frantically away, disappearing into the tangle of sagebrush at the edge of the yard. I searched for it there, parting the gray branches, peering into the shadows, but it had vanished completely. There was no trace of it—no feather, no movement, no sign whether it had settled somewhere to recover or crept off to die.

And so I was left standing among the sagebrush with my empty hands and my unanswered question. Whether the bird lived or died, whether it flew off whole into the morning or perished quietly beneath some bush, I would never know. It was, I understood then, entirely beyond me—beyond my control, beyond my knowledge. I had touched it once, and then it was gone, carried off into a fate that was never mine to decide.
outputs.L5:
# The Italian Waiter Who Changed My Trip

The small trattoria was tucked away on a narrow side street in Rome, easy to miss if you weren't paying attention. I almost walked past it entirely, but the aroma drifting from the doorway pulled me inside like an invisible hand.

The Italian waiter who greeted me was a man in his sixties, with silver hair and eyes that crinkled warmly when he smiled. He was, without question, the most attentive host I had ever encountered. There was no menu handed over in silence, no rushed recommendation. Instead, he sat down beside me and asked what I was in the mood for.

"The pasta here," he said proudly, "is made fresh every morning by my wife." His accent was thick, his English imperfect, but his passion needed no translation.

What followed was one of the finest meals of my life. The homemade tagliatelle arrived steaming, glistening with olive oil and dotted with fresh basil. Each bite was a revelation. The Italian tradition of slow, thoughtful cooking was evident in every ingredient.

By the end of the evening, I understood something important. The meal was memorable, yes, but it was the human connection that truly mattered. The Italian way of treating strangers like family had turned an ordinary dinner into a cherished memory.

I left a generous tip and a promise to return. The waiter waved from the doorway as I walked into the warm Roman night, and I realized that the best souvenirs are never things you can pack in a suitcase.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short first-person literary vignette about waking up to a bird hitting your window, and what you do about it. Make it wry and reflective.
counterfactuals.output:
The Visitor

The thud came at 6:47 a.m., which I know because I looked at my phone before I looked at anything worth looking at, which tells you something about me and about mornings.

For a moment I lay there constructing theories. Someone knocking. A branch. The universe, finally, coming to collect on some outstanding debt. Then it came again—softer, apologetic—and I understood it was a bird, throwing itself against the glass with the particular determination of a creature who has mistaken a reflection for a rival, or a doorway, or perhaps just a better version of its own life.

I get that. I have thrown myself at plenty of windows I believed were doors.

I went to the kitchen window and there it was: a small brown thing, unremarkable in every way except its persistence. A sparrow, I decided, though I have never been able to tell one small brown bird from another and have stopped pretending. It hovered, retreated, and struck the pane again, tapping out some message in a Morse code I was not qualified to receive.

The responsible thing, I knew, was to do something. Close the curtains, so the reflection would vanish. Tape a paper hawk to the glass, the way the internet suggests, as if birds were reasonable creatures who read warnings. I stood there holding my coffee and did neither. I watched.

Because here is the shameful truth: it was the most interesting thing that had happened to me in a week. I have a job and a calendar and a list of small tasks I perform in order to feel that time is passing usefully. And a bird was flinging its entire body against my window for reasons it could not name, and I recognized the gesture the way you recognize a face in a crowd—not a friend, exactly, but someone from the old neighborhood.

Eventually I drew the curtain. The tapping stopped. I felt the specific guilt of having solved a problem by removing myself from it, which is, I've noticed, my preferred method for most things.

I finished my coffee. Somewhere out there the bird had already forgotten the window, forgotten the rival that was only ever itself, and gone off to hurl itself at some other pane of the incomprehensible world.

I envied it, a little. At least it kept trying the glass.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a personal essay-style piece about a small encounter with an injured flicker outside my house, blending humor, mortality, and detachment.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Flicker**

There is a bird dying on my walkway and I am eating a granola bar.

I want to be clear that these two facts are not causally related. I did not do this to the bird. But I mention the granola bar because it seems important to the record that at the moment I discovered mortality laid out across my concrete like a dropped scarf, I had a mouth full of oats and what the wrapper insisted was "honey almond."

The bird is a flicker. I know this only because I looked it up, standing there, thumb-typing "spotted brown woodpecker chest polka dots" into a search engine while the actual creature sat six feet away doing the slow work of leaving its body. This is, I think, the most modern thing a person can do: stand beside a death and fact-check it.

The flicker had flown into my window. There was a soft, terrible thump earlier that I'd registered and then un-registered, the way you do with sounds that ask something of you. A thump is a question. I had answered it with silence and gone back to my email.

Now here it was, the consequence of the thump, tucked against the step. Its eyes had that filmed, elsewhere quality. One wing was held slightly wrong. It did not try to flee when I crouched, which was how I knew. Healthy things flee. Only the doomed and the tame let you get close, and I could not tell which this bird had become.

I did not know what to do, so I did what I always do when I don't know what to do, which is nothing, but with great attention.

I considered a box. People are always putting injured birds in boxes. I have seen this in movies and in the folk wisdom of women who wear gardening gloves unironically. A box, a towel, a dark quiet place. But I stood there calculating the logistics—which box, do I dump out the winter hats, then what, do I drive it somewhere, is there a place, is there a *building* where they take the birds—and in the calculation I understood that I was not going to do any of it. I was going to stand here and narrate.

This is the detachment I've never been able to fully explain to people who love me. In moments that call for feeling, I go instead to the balcony of myself and lean over the railing to watch. The flicker is dying and part of me is already composing the sentence about it. That part of me is a little ashamed and mostly not.

I finished the granola bar. I want that in the record too.

The thing about a bird's death is that it is enormous to the bird and roughly nothing to the world. No sirens. The mail still came. Somewhere a man was buying a boat. The flicker's whole life—the miles of it, the hollow bones engineered across millennia for a single miraculous purpose, the specific brown-and-spotted improbability of it—was concluding on my walkway between the recycling bin and a dead potted geranium I keep meaning to deal with. I keep meaning to deal with a lot of things. The geranium. The bird. My own eventual thump against some window I won't see coming.

I sat down on the step, finally. Not to help. There was no help. I sat because it seemed rude to keep standing over it like a bad landlord. If you cannot save a thing, you can at least not loom.

We stayed like that. Me and the flicker, both of us fairly certain how this was going to go. I did not narrate anymore. I just watched its chest, the polka dots rising and falling, and then rising and falling less, and then—not with any drama, no final flutter, nothing cinematic—simply holding still in a way that was categorically different from before.

Stillness has a threshold. You'd be surprised how clearly you can see it crossed.

I buried it under the geranium, which I finally dealt with. Two problems, one hole. The flicker would have appreciated the efficiency, I think, or would have appreciated nothing, being a bird and now not even that.

I went back inside and washed my hands for a long time and could not have told you why. There was no blood. I think I was washing off the balcony, the part of me that watched instead of wept, trying to get down to whatever was underneath—the part that had, at some point in the sitting, gone quiet and simply kept a small brown thing company while it left.

That part didn't narrate anything. That part is still, if I'm honest, out there on the step.

The granola bar was excellent. I'm sorry. It was.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical prose paragraph in the voice of someone living in the rural West who finds a stunned bird and contemplates whether to intervene. End with a dark, ironic observation about ants.
counterfactuals.output: The starling struck the window at first light, and now it lies in the dust of my yard like a dropped thing, like something the sky decided it no longer wanted. Its eye is a black bead of terror, its wing cocked at an angle wings were never meant to hold, and I stand over it in my boots with the mountains going pink behind me, wondering if mercy is a thing you give or a thing you only imagine giving. I could cup it in my hands, could carry it inside to a shoebox lined with an old flannel shirt, could play at being God for an afternoon—but I have seen how this goes, have buried enough small warmth in the cold ground to know that my wanting a thing to live has never once been the deciding vote. The bird shudders. Somewhere a hawk is drawing its slow circle. And the wind comes down off the ridge smelling of sage and snowmelt, indifferent as it has always been to what breathes and what does not. So I turn back toward the house and leave it to whatever comes, because out here the wanting is mine alone to carry, and the ants, at least, have already made up their minds—they arrive not to mourn but to inherit, and to them a dying thing and a feast are simply the same good fortune wearing two different faces.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a piece of flash nonfiction that captures a mundane morning moment involving nature—a bird, sagebrush, bark beetles—with a philosophical, slightly self-mocking tone.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Authority of Sparrows

There is a sparrow on my fence this morning, and it does not care that I have theories about it.

I have been standing at the kitchen window for four minutes, coffee going lukewarm in my hand, constructing a small philosophy of the sparrow. It has landed on the same weathered post three mornings running, and I have decided this means something. Ritual, perhaps. Territory. Some avian equivalent of my own compulsion to stand here every day watching a bird pretend I've decoded it.

The sagebrush beyond the fence smells like it always smells after a cold night—sharp, medicinal, like the desert clearing its throat. I read once that the scent is a chemical defense, that the plant is essentially screaming at insects in a language of volatile oils. I found this beautiful when I learned it. I told people at a party. *The sagebrush is screaming,* I said, holding my wine, feeling profound. Nobody was moved. The sagebrush, notably, was not screaming for my benefit either. It has been defending itself for millennia without an audience, which is more than I can say for most of my opinions.

In the pine at the property line, the bark beetles are doing their patient arithmetic beneath the bark, tunneling their galleries in a script no one reads until the tree is already dead. I know the tree is dying. I have known for a season. Each morning I look at it and think, *today I will call someone,* and each morning the beetles continue their work with a diligence I cannot muster for my own affairs. There is something humbling about being outworked by an insect the size of a rice grain. They do not stand at windows. They do not narrate.

The sparrow shifts its weight. I lean forward, certain now that it is about to do something meaningful.

It flies away. Not toward anything. Not away from anything I can see. It simply leaves, the way a thought leaves when you reach for a pen, and the fence post is just a fence post again, gray and splintering and holding up nothing but the morning.

I finish my cold coffee. The sagebrush goes on screaming its silent screams. The beetles keep their appointment with the tree.

And I—the only creature here who needed the moment to *mean* something—go back inside to write it down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short creative narrative that starts with being woken by a bird striking a window and moves through the narrator's ambivalent, sleepy attempt to help it, ending with the realization that its fate is "none of my business."
counterfactuals.output:
The Bird

The sound arrived before I understood it—a soft, terrible thud against the glass, then nothing. I surfaced from sleep the way you rise through deep water, slow and resistant, the dream still clinging to my ankles.

Another thump. I lay there, one eye open, watching the gray light pool on the ceiling. *A bird,* my mind offered, unhelpfully, and then curled back toward sleep like a cat.

But the sound came again, insistent, and something in me—some vestigial sense of obligation—swung my legs over the side of the bed. The floor was cold. I hated the floor for being cold. I hated the bird, a little, for requiring this of me at an hour I had not agreed to.

At the window I saw it: a small brown thing, a sparrow maybe, hurling itself at its own reflection. Again and again it lifted, hovered, and struck the glass, as if the world it wanted lived just on the other side of me. Its wings beat a frantic Morse code I couldn't read.

*I should help,* I thought. But how? Open the window and it would only fly inside, into a worse trap of walls and ceilings. Draw the curtain and I'd be sending it away without explanation. I pressed my palm flat against the cold pane, a useless gesture of communion, and the bird flinched back, then came again, undeterred by my enormous, godlike hand.

I stood there a long moment, caught in the gray, half-asleep and half-responsible, wanting to solve something I did not understand. The bird did not know it was fighting a reflection. It did not know I existed, or that I had risen for its sake, or that I was already growing bored of the drama.

And then, quite simply, the thought arrived: *This is none of my business.*

The bird had its own morning, its own war with itself, its own reasons folded into a body the size of my fist. It would live or it would not. It would learn the glass or it would exhaust itself against it. Either way, the outcome belonged to the bird, not to me, standing here in my cold bare feet, mistaking proximity for duty.

I let the curtain fall. I went back to bed. Somewhere behind the fabric the thudding continued for a while, softer now, or maybe I only imagined it softening. Sleep took me back before I could decide, and in the morning—the real morning, gold and ordinary—there was no bird at all. Only the smudge of it on the glass, a small oily ghost, already half-erased by the light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
